title: The Snowstorm Conversion: The Miracle of Isaiah 45:22 in a Small Methodist Chapel
seoTitle: The Snowstorm Conversion: The Miracle of Isaiah 45:22 | Charles Spurgeon
description: Read the profound story of Charles Spurgeon

content.text: The Plowing of the Soul and Theological Awakening

Charles Haddon Spurgeon was raised in a devout pastoral environment, his mind saturated with the profound teachings of Puritan theology from a very early age. Yet, despite this robust religious heritage and intellectual familiarity with the Scriptures, the young man had not experienced a personal, saving faith by his mid-teens. Between 1848 and 1850, Spurgeon entered a dark period characterized by severe spiritual agony, doubt, and an overwhelming conviction of his own depravity. He found himself in a state of active rebellion against God, feeling the crushing and unyielding weight of divine justice.

The psychological and spiritual turmoil he experienced was profound; as it was later described, God was actively "plowing his soul with ten black horses—the Ten Commandments—to then plow back with the gospel". Burdened by his own sinfulness and feeling utterly condemned by the strict demands of the moral law, the distressed teenager desperately sought spiritual relief and peace, wandering through various churches but finding no comfort for his troubled conscience.

The definitive turning point in Spurgeon's life—and a monumental moment in the history of the Christian church—arrived through what seemed to be a mere meteorological accident on Sunday morning, January 6, 1850. Spurgeon, then fifteen years old, had set out to attend a morning service at a Congregational church in the town of Colchester, hoping to find some solace for his disturbed soul.

However, a fierce and blinding snowstorm struck the region, forcing him to abandon his original route. Seeking immediate refuge from the freezing weather, he wandered down Artillery Street and slipped into a small, obscure Primitive Methodist chapel. The severe snowstorm had prevented the regular minister from arriving that morning, and the congregation that had managed to gather consisted of only a small handful of people.
The Untrained Preacher and the Divine Command

In the absence of the ordained minister, an untrained lay preacher—a simple itinerant minister named John Eeglen—stepped into the pulpit to deliver the morning message. Eeglen lacked formal theological education and possessed no polished oratorical skills, but he spoke with a nervous yet profound spiritual earnestness. He opened the Bible and read his text from the Old Testament prophet Isaiah, chapter 45, verse 22: "Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else". Looking out at the sparse gathering, the lay preacher's eyes quickly locked onto the unfamiliar teenage visitor sitting under the gallery. He immediately noticed the boy's troubled, confused, and distressed countenance.

With a striking and unexpected directness that broke all conventions of polite preaching, Eeglen pointed his finger right at Spurgeon and announced: "Young man, you look very miserable. You always will be miserable in life and miserable in death if you don't obey my text. But, if you obey now, you will be saved this moment." Following this sharp, personal diagnosis, he passionately commanded the boy to obey the text and simply look to Jesus Christ.
The Miracle of the New Birth and Its Theological Fruits

At that exact moment, the miracle of regeneration took place. Heeding the fervent appeal of the lay preacher, Spurgeon looked to Christ with faith and repentance, accepting Him as his Savior and substitute. He was instantaneously born again in the Spirit, rescued from the power of darkness, and brought safely into the kingdom of God. The heavy, agonizing burden of his sin was permanently lifted. The spiritual transformation was so visibly evident that upon returning home that same day, his mother, Eliza, saw his radiant face and instantly recognized that a wonderful change had occurred in her son. The fruit of this conversion was swift; a few months later, on May 3, 1850, Spurgeon was baptized in the River Lark by pastor W. W. Cantlow and officially joined the Baptist congregation in Newmarket.
This snowstorm conversion eternally anchored Spurgeon's theological commitment to the doctrines of grace and the sovereignty of God in salvation. Reflecting years later, Spurgeon wrote:

"I took no torch with which to light the sun; but the sun enlightened me. I did not commence my spiritual life,—no, I rather kicked and struggled against the things of the Spirit: when He drew me, for a time I did not run after Him."

He realized that his salvation was a miraculous intervention of divine grace. The text of Isaiah 45:22 remained the central pillar of his personal identity and his public proclamation throughout his life. Its significance was so monumental that forty-two years later, during his massive funeral in February 1892, six thousand mourners filed past his casket, before which was reverently displayed the very Bible verse that God had used to convert the man who would become the greatest preacher of the Victorian era.
